articles.text: A report delivered to City Council last week detailed an unusually high amount of overtime in the Piedmont Fire Department. During the annual midyear financial report presented on Tuesday, February 20, City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore and Finance Director Michael Szczech explained that because of understaffing problems, which have plagued the department for several years, firefighters have had to work more overtime than typical. As a result, City Council has authorized an additional $125,000 to cover overtime costs through the end of the fiscal year. Szczech said that the overtime costs are mostly offset by the lower number of employees. Though the problem has been resolved in recent months and the department is now fully staffed, Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan said the period of low staffing and long hours had contributed to low morale at the station. Szczech sounded cautiously optimistic in his assessment of the Fire Department’s financial future. “The department, which was down as many as seven employees at one point, is now fully staffed. However, three of the new employees are attending the fire academy. So, overtime will continue to be high, but to a lesser extent in the second half of the year,” he said. “All fire departments are short right now,” explained Brannigan. Since the pandemic, there have been nationwide shortages of firefighters across the country, including in Piedmont. “It was very difficult for our current employees from late spring of 2023 until right about New Year’s this year. People were working a lot of extra shifts, and it was really starting to impact morale in their families.” Matters seem to have improved though, said Brannigan, with the addition of seven new hires in recent months. “It’s been challenging for sure, but we got some relief in December, and it’s much more manageable now,” he said. To prevent personnel shortages in the future, the department has adopted a proactive hiring policy. “We are working on ongoing recruitment, which is not something we’ve had to do in the past. We have more outreach going on and more defined communication paths with potential candidates. That brought in a bigger pool of qualified applicants and we now have a current list to draw from if needed more quickly,” said Brannigan.

articles.text: Editor: The evidence lies all around us of what under-funded municipalities look like. As a lifelong resident of the East Bay, what I’m seeing in our surrounding communities is demoralizing. While especially noticeable in emergency services, the deterioration appears to have impacted all civil services. The root cause may be debatable, but the one common complaint is funding, and lack thereof. Piedmont is an exception. Our police and fire departments still “work.” Our parks are maintained, and our recreation department continues to meet our needs. I’m grateful. Measure F maintains and improves the City services that we depend upon. Without it cuts will be made. Make no mistake. It won’t just be in our public security; it will be in other less appreciated amenities like our library contract with Oakland. Now more than ever, we need to protect city services. I join our City Council and strongly encourage passage of Measure F. –Chris Hart

articles.text: By: Hari Titan, Ph.D. Student enrollment has been going down due to 1) a declining birth rate, 2) increased expense for families to move to Piedmont, 3) families who can afford private schools, and 4) empty-nesters who remain in Piedmont. PUSD presented a budget workshop on January 11 to discuss possible cuts that would achieve the cost-of-living-adjustment (COLA) the union was seeking. Out of fear of a strike, I decided to analyze past budgets (bit.ly/PUSDBudget) myself and found a number of interesting things which I presented to district leadership. PUSD enrollment declined 14.8% (2014-23) despite a total funding increase of 47% over the same time period. This student enrollment decline was roughly 8% above the state’s average decline rate of 6.7%. State income taxes (including capital gains tax) went up much higher over those years and a fixed percentage of that goes toward TK-12 education. Had that not occurred, revenue from the state could have been roughly 8% higher. That’s the revenue “loss” referred to by PUSD in recent documents. The schools don’t really need that extra money because there are fewer students to support. Logically, if enrollment goes down by 8%, staff should correspondingly go down by a similar percentage. Deciding which smaller classes to merge and which staff to reduce is not easy. The resulting savings would help cover the COLA. Property taxes and our parcel taxes act as a bit of a buffer on the rightsizing needed since those funding sources are locked in for 8 years, independent of enrollment changes. I urge the community to review the Budget Workshop presentation attached to the January 11th board meeting. The presentation had a slide that revealed the downward enrollment trend, grade by grade. 12th and 11th grades in 2023 are well above 200 students, middle school grades are below 190, elementary grades below 175, with 1st and 2nd grades below 160 and the Kindergarten class at 135 students. Lower enrollment isn’t temporary and requires addressing staffing levels, not papered over with higher parcel taxes. The City Services Tax funds core city services, includ- ing police, fire and paramedic services, the maintenance of parks, green spaces, stormwater, infrastructure, streets and public facilities, in addition to planning, library, recreation and other community services. The BAFPC evaluated the City’s 10-year financial projections and maintenance needs, concluding that long-term stable funding is essential for city services. The City Council took action to place the renewal of the tax on the March 5, 2024, ballot. The ballot measure proposes a 20% increase and a 12-year term to preserve existing service levels citywide, augment staffing for the emergency 911 communication center, and leverage new and improved technology. Measure F amounts to an estimated increase of less than $15 per month for most property owners. articles.text: Public Works estimates work to be completed by April 5 Residents may not have to worry about construction on Oakland Avenue much longer. The Piedmont Public Works Department has confirmed that the installation of the project to install bulb-outs at three intersections is on-track to finish by April 5. Construction workers are currently installing bulb-outs at the corners of Jerome Avenue and Oakland Avenue, El Cerrito and Oakland Avenue, and Nova and Magnolia Avenue. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that two bulb-outs have already been poured at each of the intersections of Jerome and El Cerrito. The third location is a Y-intersection at Nova and Magnolia Avenue, where a former cluster of bollards has been removed. The total construction cost for this project is $773,885. Project funding includes a $50,000 contribution from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation and approximately $600,000 from the State Gas Tax. “The increased [crime] activity is part of the formula, but we have always been understaffed with primarily one dispatcher on at any time that works the window, answers non-emergency and 911, while talking with the Police Department, Fire Department, and any other sources needed to support them. That can be overloading when something significant happens,” said Captain Chris Monahan. The first dispatcher position was filled earlier this month by new hire Rachel Ponce, who is currently in training. articles.text: Editor: Like so many others, am writing to express my strong support for Measure F. I know that sometimes it can feel like we’re pouring our (often large) tax contributions down a drain, that we’re throwing money into an oncoming tide of problems that we have very little ability to fix. But one of the many benefits of living in Piedmont is we get to be the direct beneficiaries of our local taxes. Our already outstanding emergency services will be made better by Measure F, and we will be even safer. Our streets will be even more beautiful. There will be even more shared space in which to enjoy our friends, neighbors, and larger community. Our recreation options will be even better. I urge everyone to vote yes with me on Measure F. –Max Roman
articles.title: Voicing strong support for Measure F

articles.text: As Piedmont residents for 50 years, we fully support Ken Berrick for the AC Transit Board of Supervisors. We have known Ken for over 30 years and know his lifelong advocacy and work with children, mental health, education, social services, and housing. Ken was the founder and CEO of Seneca Center, providing these services throughout the County and State. He worked closely with Counties and their departments on all levels to develop innovative programs which maximized Federal dollars and ensured successful outcomes. This election is not just about one issue. We have multiple issues that require expertise to solve. It’s about holding the County and its staff accountable and maximizing resources to get the job done. It’s about outcomes and follow through. Ken Berrick has done this in his work and will do this as a Board of Supervisor. Having worked with Ken as a fellow service provider in multiple Counties throughout the State, I can personally attest to Ken’s forward thinking and follow-through as well as his expertise in County and State issues and effective solutions. We cannot be swayed by emotions. We need to think strategically about who can win and do the best job for us, our district and County. Ken Berrick is the more viable candidate throughout our district. A vote for Chris will result in neither Chris or Ken being elected and open the election for an unwanted candidate from Oakland being elected. Let’s not let what happened in the Oakland Mayor’s election happen with this Board of Supervisors election. Vote for Ken Berrick for AC Board of Supervisor. –Mary Jane & Benton Gross Piedmont Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. Subscribe to the Post and we’ll deliver

articles.text: Photo by April Fitzgerald Officer Jessica Morey next to a police patrol car Community members may have seen new police office Jessica Morey, a former teacher, as she patrols city streets and at Cop on the Block events. “I was a teacher in a classroom for preschool-aged students,” she said in an interview, explaining there were similar motivations between the two careers. “It really does come down to the fact that I like helping people,” she said. On January 8 the PPD announced that Officer Morey completed her field training program, making her a fully sworn officer on the force. It is an achievement she is proud of and welcomes the responsibility. “I just feel very, very welcomed here. I’m happy to be here and start my journey as a sworn officer,” she said. Morey grew up in San Mateo and attended Carlmont High School. She went on to study at San Jose State University, where she earned a B.S. in Child and Adolescent Development. While she was in college, she taught preschool students and supervised children in an afterschool care program but overall felt that something was missing. “In my last semester I took a criminal justice class, and that’s when I realized after a few years of teaching I really wanted to do police work her way instead.” Morey found Piedmont based upon the recommendation of a friend. She was working as a Community Service Officer in the San Jose Police Department when a colleague approached her and her best friend, Ashley Gallion, now also a Piedmont Police officer. “He knew we both wanted to go sworn, and he put us in contact with Capt. Chris Monahan,” she said. Officer Morey remembers that during her first ride-along in Piedmont, it was a culture shock compared to her time in San Jose. “I remember driving with Officer Petit and Officer Diaz thinking that the city was so cute, and then Officer Diaz started rolling down the window and waving to everybody. In San Jose, people don’t wave at you unless they’re trying to get your attention or have you stop for them.” Morey said the interaction left an impression on her. “That was huge. [Ashley and I] applied as soon as we could, and then luck worked out that we both got hired.” She said she appreciates the culture of community policing in Piedmont. “I’m not just a name or a badge number in this city. I’m a face with a name and people will want to get to know me.”

articles.text: The City of Piedmont invites community members to apply for vacancies on seven commissions and committees. These volunteer positions serve as a way to learn more about the inner workings of City government and to become involved in local government. These positions will regularly hear reports from City staff about current and proposed services, policies, and programs and will help shape the direction these bodies take by providing valuable insight and resident perspectives. All vacant offices serve threeyear terms subject to a limit of two consecutive terms. Residents may apply online at www.piedmont.ca.gov/commissioner. Vacancies on the following commissions and committees will be available: Park Commission – Advises City Council on issues related to public parks and street trees. The commission meets regularly on the first Wednesday of the month at 5:30 p.m. The Park Commission currently has two vacancies and two incumbents on the commission are currently eligible to reapply. Planning Commission – Advises City Council on issues related to planning and building and makes decisions regarding proposed modifications or construction to homes. This commission requires approximately four hours per month in addition to its scheduled meeting time. The commission meets regularly on the second Monday of the month at 5:30 p.m. The Planning Commission has one vacancy and no incumbents on the commission are currently eligible to reapply. Recreation Commission – Advises City Council on issues regarding recreation programs, sports field development, allocations of field space, and other related issues. The commission meets on the third Wednesday of the month at 7:30 p.m. The commission has two vacancies and one incumbent on the commission is currently eligible to reapply. Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee – Provides recommendations on the City’s annual budget, long-term financial projections, mid-year budget adjustments, and the City’s municipal services tax rate and renewal. The committee meets as needed. The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee currently has two vacancies and two incumbents on the committee are currently eligible to reapply. Public Safety Committee – Advises on efforts to increase public participation in crime reduction and disaster preparedness. The committee meets quarterly, has two vacancies and one incumbent on the committee is currently eligible to reapply. Police and Fire Pension Board – Oversees the investment of funds in the legacy pension plan for Police Officers and Firefighters. The board meets quarterly. The Police and Fire Pension Board has one vacancy and one incumbent on the commission is currently eligible to reapply. Civil Service Commission – Oversees personnel issues (including classification) and serves as the hearing board in disputes between the City and employees. The commission meets as needed. The Civil Service Commission currently has two vacancies and two incumbents on the commission are currently eligible to reapply. Applications are due by 5 p.m. on Friday, March 15. The City Council will appoint a total of 12 seats. Applicants must attend an in-person interview at City offices in the evening of Monday, March 25, to be considered for appointment. Interviews will be conducted by the City Council and will last roughly five minutes each. The interview schedule will be provided to applicants on Friday, March 22. For more information, contact the City Clerk’s office at 420-3040 or e-mail at cityclerk@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: During a Piedmont School Board meeting on February 14, the school district announced a limited time incentive for teachers for early retirement of resignation – a one-time $40,000 payment, for veteran teachers at the top of the pay scale. The school district placed a deadline of Monday, February 26 for a decision. A minimum of 10 staff positions would be required to complete the offer. As of February 27, the school district had not receive enough applicants and the program will not be in effect. The proposal was contingent upon receiving that number to make the saving meaningful for the district. As of February 14, the district had around 30 teachers with senior qualifications, either on the maximum step and column of their salary schedule, or having been with the district more than 20 years. “I don’t think the objective was to reduce our teaching ranks, because we would be refilling.” said Finance Director Ruth Alahydoian. Employees that may have submitted their intent may rescind their retirement/resignation since the incentive program did not fulfill its requirements. The program was projected to save the district $100,000 in future years, with the $40,000 payments guaranteed by Piedmont Education Foundation. The typical advance notice date for teachers to retire was February 15. During the school board meeting, board members applauded the program as creative and a win-win, although board member Cory Smegal worried the deadline was too soon given Ski Week ending one day prior. The now failed proposal was also offered as a tantalizing option to limit the number of March 15 salary reduction notices that would be sent to teachers. “This offer is possible this year due to unique circumstances and is not likely to be available in future years,” the board document read.

articles.text: Linda Beach Cooperative Preschool welcomes families from Piedmont, Oakland and Berkeley and surrounding areas to an Open House on Saturday, March 16 from 10 a.m.-12 p.m. Parents are welcome to tour the warm and welcoming classroom and have a chance to meet the teachers and other families. The preschool has been a Piedmont fixture for more than 80 years. The school emphasizes the development of each child through independent and group play-based activities. Classroom adults always include two teachers and two or three parent volunteers. This allows for a maximum 5:1 child to adult ratio. LBCP offers gymnastics classes that allow for children to grow better body awareness and strengthen their gross motor skills. The M/W/F (4 year old) program also provides Spanish classes where children are introduced to the Spanish language and culture by native Spanish-speaking adults. Families are encouraged to participate in field trips to Tilden’s Little Farm, the Piedmont Fire Station, and Roberts Park. The cooperative preschool not only provides families the opportunity to watch their child grow in the classroom, but it also allows families to build and further develop their parent network. Through the experience of classroom participation, approximately once a month, parents have the unique opportunity to see their child in the context of their peers and to receive feedback from teachers and other parents about their child. All LBCP teachers became involved with Linda Beach as parents. The much-loved director, Shelley Kelly, has been an integral part of the school for 32 years. She is also the lead teacher for the 3-year old program and assists the 4-year old classroom. To sign up, take a tour, or learn more about Linda Beach Cooperative Preschool, visit Lindabeach. org.

articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation has announced that this year’s Spring Fling will be co-chaired by three elementary school dads, Marco Gonzalez-Navarro (Havens), Michael Gross (Beach), and Max Roman (Wildwood). “This is our chance to ensure that essential programs are not lost, whether donating an item for the auction, organizing a parent-sponsored party, or coming to the Spring Fling Gala to bid.” said Gross, who is the President of Beach School Dads Club. “Last year’s Spring Fling raised enough to fund expanded counseling and lunchtime library coverage,” said Roman. PEF and the co-chairs aim for an exciting event schedule. This year’s Gala is scheduled for Saturday, May 4, in Oakland’s Jack London Square with a theme of an evening in Venice. “We hope parents have a fantastic time with friends and neighbors while showing how much we all support and care for Piedmont schools,” said Gonzalez-Navaro. Volunteers are putting together theme parties such as Aloha to 5th Grade, High Chai Tea, and Spin and Sip – all benefitting the elementary schools. articles.text: Camp Joyful Voices is a sleepaway experience for 7-10 year olds Registration is now open for Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir summer music camp, where kids get to sing under the stars with their friends. Camp Joyful Voices, the choir’s popular camp program for singers ages 7-10, has added a second week by popular demand and spaces are filling quickly. Created with young singers in mind, this weeklong sleepaway camp is the perfect opportunity for children to build confidence, deepen musical skills, and make new friends. Children are encouraged to sing on hikes, at Turtle Pond, and around the campfire at night. Singers share cabins, compete for prizes for creative outfits during Spirit Days, and spend time reading, napping, writing letters, playing games, and bonding with each other. They swim and kayak at Turtle Pond, go on hikes to explore nature, watch sunsets, do arts and crafts, and share camp recitals and evening programs. By the time the last day of camp rolls around, the joy and memories are mixed with not wanting to leave. Join us this summer; we can’t wait to sing with you. articles.text: Staff Photos Coach Ben Spencer’s boys’ basketball team fell to University in the Div. 3 NCS Finals but qualified for the State Tournament. Piedmont High’s championship dreams fell short on Friday, February 23, as the boys’ basketball team, the No. 3 seed, fell to No. 1 seed University 65-55 in the Division 3 North Coast Section Finals at the University of San Francisco. On the way to the finals they defeated No. 2 Archie Williams 64-61 in San Anselmo on Tuesday, February 20. It was a great response to Piedmont’s early-season 93-61 loss to University on December 12, and coach Ben Spencer considers this year’s team one of the most special he’ has coached. “[University’s] press was a challenge for us in the fourth quarter. I’m not sure which team I’m more proud of—this team or the NCS Championship team we had [in 2020]. It’s a tossup. This group lost to University by 32 points [ in December]. As coaches and players we challenged each other the rest of the way to play 100 percent every game. For the next 24 games, we did that. We were right there,” he said. But Piedmont’s season isn’t over. By reaching the North Coast Section finals, they automatically qualified for the CIF State Tournament. They were placed in Div. 3 as the No. 14 seed and on Tuesday night, February 27, they faced Valley Christian in San Jose. Results were not available at press time. The game was back and forth with Piedmont holding leads briefly in the third and fourth quarters, including a 42-41 lead after Ravi Silverberg knocked down a 3-pointer to open the fourth quarter. Silverberg led the scoring with 23 points and senior leader Brit Burden finished with 16. The Red Devils kept a heavy press on the Highlanders through all four quarters, which Piedmont dealt well with until fatigue started to show during the late part of the game. PHS committed six turnovers in the final quarter. “Once the game started, I knew I had to be aggressive and my shots started falling, so I just kept shooting,” said Silverberg. “They’d trap in the post and have a second guy in the post, so it was tough to get inside. They had a great game plan and they were really good on-ball defenders,” said Burden. Burden had one of the best NCS semifinals performances in the last 10 years with 28 points in the semifinal win over Archie Williams, rarely missing when attacking the rim for layups. The 64-61 semifinal score looks a lot closer than the game actually was. PHS held a 52-33 lead entering the fourth quarter. The Peregrine Falcons landed a flurry of three-point shots in the final few minutes. “Brit’s performance was up there; he was a force. He set the tone early by going to the basket and drawing fouls. We just played physical against Archie. it was an unbelievable performance and hopefully we still have more basketball left,” added Spencer. 65-55 to University After a defensive first quarter, Piedmont led 10-9. The offense was going strong in the second quarter when Silverberg hit a 3-pointer to take a 20-19 lead at the 3:07 mark. But University went on a 10-0 run to take a 29-20 lead at halftime. In the third quarter, the Highlanders rallied with a 16-5 run to move in front 35-34 with 2:25 left. But University quickly responded with a layup and free throw by Gus Fried to go back ahead 37-35. Burden put Piedmont in the lead at 39-38 on a layup with 1:20 to go, but University’s Gus Parsons hit a 3-pointer to make it 41-39 Red Devils. Piedmont came out firing in the fourth with Arjun Bornstein feeding Silverberg for a 3-pointer to give the Highlanders a 42-41 lead 10 seconds into the quarter. It was the last time they held the lead. The Red Devils quickly got back in front with a pair of free throws by Cole Boake for the start of a 13-2 run that put University up 54-44. Both teams traded baskets in the remaining time, including five free throws by Burden and Silverberg with a pair of three-pointers. Final stats: Silverberg had 23 points, Burden had 16 points, Thorin Holmes and Dillon Casey both had six, Declan Linnane scored four. 64-41 over Archie Williams Piedmont got out to a 16-11 lead and led 37-23 at halftime. The Highlanders extended the lead to 52-33 entering the fourth quarter, while the Peregrin Falcons scored 28 points in the final Ravi Silverberg led scoring in the finals with 23 points against University.

articles.text: Piedmont’s track & field team sent three athletes to the 18th annual Skyline Invitational in Oakland on Saturday, February 24: sophomore pole vaulter Marcos Arno, senior sprinter and long jumper Breah Bell, and junior Sam Shelby making his season debut. Much of the PHS team was out of town for Ski Week. Shelby started his season in a big way. He finished fourth in the 100 meters in a field of 144 athletes with a time of 11.34. He’s poised for a strong spring season after a breakout campaign on the football team last fall, He was named WACC Offensive Player of the Year and an All-Metro selection by the SF Chronicle. “Sam picked up right where he left off in the 100m, missing his end of season PR by less than a tenth of a second,” said coach Pouyan Assadi. “He has more power than ever, so now we just need to build up his endurance and we’ll be good.” Photo by Becky Swain Breah Bell competed in the 100 meters, long jump and triple jump at the Skyline Invitational. Sam Shelby made his season debut in the 100 and 200 meters and in the long jump. Sprinter and relay runner Sam Shelby (second from right). Shelby also ran the 200 meters, placing 14th of 142 sprinters with a time of 23.81 seconds. He also made his high school debut in the long jump, placing ninth of 59 jumpers with a distance of 19 feet, 6.5 inches, a mark that was eighth best over the last decade at Piedmont High. “We pushed Sam to consider a third individual event and long jump makes sense. He comes down the runway with tons of velocity and after maybe just three hours total of long jump practice, he’s already just a couple steps away being an elite jumper. Saturday was the first time he ever officially jumped,” Assadi said. Bell, now a senior, competed in three events. She placed 14th of 114 athletes in the 100 meter dash with a time of 13.34.“ Breah blasted out of the blocks with more power and better form than I’ve ever seen from her. Now we just have to work on endurance and we’ll be cooking,” Assadi said. She was also 12th of 24 in the long jump at 15 feet, one inch, and 11th of 17 in the triple jump in 29 feet, 1.75 inches. “Breah is still working on the mechanics of her jumps, but her confidence is there and we like the direction she’s headed,” Assadi said. Arno, a sophomore, was ninth of 13 in the pole vault with a height of eight feet, seven inches. NEXT UP Piedmont will compete in the Dan Gabor Invitational at Amador Valley HS in Pleasanton on Saturday, March 2 at 8:30 a.m.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team starts its season after reaching the North Coast Section finals last year. They lost 11-10 in double overtime to Tamalpais. The Highlanders compiled a 14-4 record last season and won their sixth consecutive Western Alameda County Conference championship. A big change is underway, however. This year’s team has a new head coach, Jeff Lamb. Coach Al Yu unexpectedly left the team a few months ago. Lamb competed at Georgetown University during his college career. He coached at Arlington after graduating in 2012. Ny day he is Vice President of Seven Post Investment. “I grew up on the East Coast and received a scholarship to play at Georgetown. I played two years as a midfielder but fractured my femur, which put a stop to my playing career. After I graduated, I was an assistant at Washington-Liberty High School in Arlington, Virginia,” Lamb said. “I moved to the Bay Area about 10 years ago and made the move to Alameda. After a series of introductions and relationships with some parents in Piedmont with children in high school, they found out I played lacrosse in college. They asked if I was interested. I’ve always loved coaching and love the sport, so I wanted to lend a hand,” he added. Boys’ lacrosse has become one of the school’s top performing teams over the last decade and Lamb acknowledged the pressure to be quickly successful at Piedmont High. “The expectation levels are high. The reality is there were quite a few seniors who graduated. One of the important things is getting the new players and mid-level experienced players as Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team returns to Witter Field after reaching last year’s North Coast Section finals. articles.text: Piedmont MTB is back after racing in the Fun at the Fort event at Fort Ord to open its season. Pictured are Schuyler Sawicki (left), Max Rivera, and Mark Hsia after their varsity race Piedmont’s Mountain Bike team made its season debut on a bright and sunny Saturday, February 24, at the Fun at the Fort event at Fort Ord in the National Interscholastic Cycling League’s NorCal East Bay/Central Region. They brought 10 athletes which was raced on a four-mile course. In the five-lap varsity event, Max Rivera led the way for Piedmont by finishing 24th of 41 with a time of 1:18:53.64. Behind him was Mark Hsia in 25th, clocking a 1:19:03.50. Schuyler Sawicki was 34th with a time of 1:20:17.62, while Scanu came in 1:30:13.17. During the race, Scanu took a hard fall on the second lap. Rivera, Hsia, and Sawicki rode in a close pack on their way to the finish. Piedmont had two athletes in the four-lap JV1 race. Jasper Schuetz finished 12th of 45 in 1:02:53.06 after being hampered by a cold. Schuetz notably won nearly every event of last year in the sophomore category. Cary Ward, meanwhile, was close behind in 14th in 1:03:50.84. In the JV2 race, sophomores Caleb Canada and Asher Villarreal competed. Canada was 29th of 50 in 57:12.74 while Villareal was 45th in 1:11:06.86. Olive Reining raced in the girls’ JV2 race, clocking a 1:25:09.27. Piedmont’s MTB Junior Development team middle school riders also competed at Fort Ord on a shorter course. 8th grade rider Josephine Schuetz was ninth of 12 in 44:28.12. Rose Reining finished in 47:13.24. Sixth grade riders making their debut included Carter Lew in 22nd of 58, and Quincy Aguilar, who was 43rd in 31:21.73. articles.text: San Francisco corps de ballet on opening night of Swan Lake. A wondrous night unfolded at the Opera House as the S.F. Ballet’s swans floated in gracefully and flew off to the cheers of a sold-out house. For many, “Swan Lake” is the pinnacle of all ballet love-drama fantasies, a fairy tale that grips the heart with great endearment. This time with a very promising ballerina out of Sweden, Nikisha Fogo. The fairy-tale plot: innocent maidens are scooped up by the evil winged sorcerer Von Rothbart, transformed magically into swans, and subservient into all eternity. Subplot is a fickle human swain of lesser IQ, Prince Siegfried, falling in love with her, and later falling for the bot, Rothbart’s seductive look-alike Black Swan, the super-athlete, which leads to the demise of one and all, and to wet hankies throughout the house. “Well, yeah,” said the wise one. “But actually I read it as allegory, Rothbart being the bully major power swallowing up the less powerful defenseless neighbor in a quick war, like a shark after minnows.” Hmmmm…. Fairy tale or Weltpolitik, even after a century and a half, the “Swan Lake” experience conquers hearts and souls around the world while offering the dream role for all aspiring ballerinas. The opening night’s wronged heroine, Odette/Odile, was Fogo. Initially a habile technician in that tremulous first meeting with the prince, Ms. Fogo became an ever more poetic presence with him in that nonpareil act two, all white with those swan feathers embracing her hair. The Black Swan role suited her even better, calling on her playing the deceitful one reverberantly, combined with the requisite endurance to make 32 whipping fouettée spins in her solo variation, one of the greatest physical challenges in all ballet. These she spun off brilliantly to the exuberant house Feb. 23, without the creeping toward the footlights that fatigue often imposes. Photos by Lindsay Thomas If Fogo is not yet the ultimate swan queen, she is well en route, beloved by the admiring throng. Her Prince was Aaron Robison, a powerful partner with soaring jetée leaps and the knack for throwing her effortlessly toward the skies. Heightening the drama are her two prescribed backward falls, each time caught adroitly by the prince. In his best role ever, corps member Nathaniel Remez flew about the stage like a black crow from first to last, nearly earning audience boos for his malevolent Rothbart role. Not to be forgotten was the parade of snow-white enchanted swans in perfect alignment, sometimes 16, sometimes up to 30, that enkindled the audience all night long. And of course the quartet of fast-stepping cygnets in their rapid-fire show-stopper – deft contrasting segment by composer Tchaikovsky. Apart from the brass section, Martin West’s orchestra was unassailable. Please join us for our upcoming in-person seminar.
articles.title: Could Swan Lake be an allegorical tale?

The two-person play follows Manuel and Johaira, a Dominican couple in New York City, as they navigate an unforeseen tragedy that upends their relationship and their lives. Johaira (Maribel Martinez) and Manuel (Xavier Pacheco) are an unlikely couple. The beautiful Johaira is an accomplished attorney and Manuel is a brutish auto mechanic, but sparks fly between them when they first meet at a club in New York City’s Washington Heights neighborhood. That meeting sets the scene for Bees & Honey, and their relationship through turmoil and tragedy. articles.text: Famed saxophonist to appear at SF Jazz Feb. 29 to March 3 Saxophonist Branford Marsalis at SF Jazz this week Branford Marsalis returns to San Francisco’s Miner Auditorium at SF Jazz tomorrow, February 29, and will perform a series of concerts through March 3. Marsalis is a highly regarded composer and jazz tenor saxophonist who comes from a lineage of jazz greats hailing from New Orleans. He is the eldest son of pianist and educator Ellis Marsalis, and his brothers Wynton, Jason and Delfeayo are all well-known musicians in the genre. Marsalis’ vast repertoire includes works by Copland, Debussy, Glazunov, Ibert, Mahler, Milhaud, Rorem, Vaughn Williams, Villa-Lobos and Sally Beamish. He is often a guest with leading symphony orchestras, and has performed with the New York Philharmonic, Chicago Symphony, Detroit Symphony, Dusseldorf Symphony, and North Carolina Symphony, Marsalis will be joined at Miner Auditorium by Joey Calderazzo on piano, Eric Revis on bass and Justin Faulkner on drums. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfjazz.org/tickets/ productions/23-24/branford-marsalis/ or call the box office at 415-788-7353. Performance times vary.

articles.text: Virginia Hong is a successful entrepreneur, an accomplished software developer, and, at her core, a genuine artist. Her journey unfolds as a passionate photographer who finds solace and inspiration in the quiet moments of life. Unlike conventional photographers, she captures moments not for the world, but for her own pleasure and meditation. She seeks out subjects and scenes that resonate with serenity, stillness, and tranquility similar to what she finds when she programs. Her large immersive prints are windows into a sanctuary of peace and quiet, inviting viewers to pause, breathe, and indulge themselves in a moment of quietude, allowing for an escape from their hectic lives. Her solo exhibit at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, amid the height of the COVID pandemic in August 2021, garnered significant attendance. Throughout 2024 the Piedmont Post will publish Hong’s photos monthly based upon her 2024 photography calendar, beginning with Emerald Bay in her series of photos of Lake Tahoe. The photo shown was taken just a short distance beyond Emerald Bay on Emerald Bay Drive. Following my sunrise session at Emerald Bay, I stumbled upon this captivating sight: a flawless reflection on the still lake, creating a fascinating texture reminiscent of arrows pointing towards the right on the horizon. Join us at the Troop 4 Open House on Monday, March 4 from 7:30-8:30 p.m. at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens School. Come discover the excitement of scouting and the countless opportunities for personal growth and outdoor exploration. Whether you’re interested in hiking, camping, or learning essential life skills, Troop 4 offers a supportive environment where boys and girls can develop leadership abilities and forge lifelong friendships. Come meet our dedicated leaders and scouts, explore our meeting place, and learn about upcoming activities. Don’t miss this chance to embark on a journey of discovery and fun with Scout Troop 4. Leadership Development Troop 4’s activities are not just about adventure and exploration; they also serve as a platform for leadership development. Through designated leadership roles within their patrols or crews, scouts have the opportunity to practice decision-making, communication, and problem-solving skills in real-world scenarios. Scout Leaders will often be the ones to take responsibility for the group; to lead their scouts to complete tasks. Guided by adult leaders and mentors, scouts learn to lead by example, inspire their peers, and navigate challenges with resilience and integrity. Water-Based activities For scouts who are drawn to aquatic adventures, activities such as canoeing, kayaking, and rafting provide exciting opportunities for skill development and exploration. Whether paddling down a peaceful river or navigating challenging whitewater rapids, scouts learn valuable lessons in teamwork, safety, and water conservation. These experiences not only build confidence in the water but also teaches scouts how to survive and use the water as an advantage in everyday life. Camping Camping lies at the heart of the Scout experience. Whether it’s a weekend getaway at a local campground or an extended expedition into the wilderness, camping trips offer scouts the chance to disconnect from technology and immerse themselves in the beauty of nature. In previous years, we camped through a lot of places such as rain and harsh weather at Sugarloaf Regional Park, American Whitewater River Rafting, and camping at the Ferguson Observatory. Moreover, camping builds teamwork and relationships between scouts as they work together to tackle challenges and share memorable experiences under the stars. You will make great memories, singing around the fire and making stories to lighten up the night sky. Snow sports From skiing to snowboarding to snowshoeing, our troop offers exciting opportunities for scouts to hone their skills on the slopes while building camaraderie and resilience. Whether carving through fresh powder or mastering the art of snowshoeing, our experienced leaders provide expert guidance to ensure safe and memorable experiences. With winter landscapes as our playground, scouts learn valuable lessons in teamwork, perseverance, and outdoor survival. Service Projects In addition to recreational activities, Scout trips often incorporate service projects that allow scouts to give back to their communities and the environment. Whether it’s participating in trail maintenance, beach cleanups, or conservation efforts, scouts learn the importance of environmental stewardship and civic responsibility. As of today, we have gone to a number of service projects, such as the Scouting for Food and the Tree Lot. Scouts not only use these service projects as a way to obtain merit badges and rank requirements, but also do them just to help the community. These service projects instill a sense of pride and purpose, empowering scouts to make a positive impact on the world around them while reinforcing the values of service and leadership. articles.text: An 8-month-old female tiger cub is now being rehabilitated at Oakland Zoo. As agents for the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, Oakland Zoo assisted with the rescue of an eight-month-old tiger cub illegally owned in the western U.S. Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital staff performed a thorough physical exam, CT scan, and bloodwork which found the female cub to have at least 10 ten improperly healed fractures. The fractures were determined to be the result of decalcification of her bones, a result of inadequate amounts of calcium and phosphorus in her diet. It resulted in the weakening of the bones and subsequent fracturing during normal young tiger activities. “I’ve treated over 100 cases of rescued big cats, and unfortunately, these injuries can lead to lifelong medical issues,” said Dr. Ryan Sadler, Senior Veterinarian at Oakland Zoo. The Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital team is working to build her calcium intake and develop a physical therapy plan to rehabilitate the atrophied muscles. Oakland Zoo is cautiously optimistic though the healing and restoration to full health will take some time. “Seeing this young tiger enduring such obvious suffering is extremely difficult. No animal should experience life in this way. We are grateful to serve in a role that gives her hope for brighter days ahead,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. Currently the tiger’s medical issues prevent her from performing natural behaviors like running and climbing. The Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital is working steadily to strengthen her through specialized enrichment. When she fully heals and is cleared medically, she will move to her new home in a large animal sanctuary. Oakland Zoo supported the federal Big Cat Public Safety Act (BCPSA), legislature approved in December 2022 that bans private ownership and public contact with big cats and imposes new restrictions on their commerce, breeding, possession, and use. BCPSA helps put an end to businesses that practice ‘cub petting’ for profit, as exemplified on the popular show “Tiger King.” Oakland Zoo underwent a thorough review by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) to obtain accreditation and has been in the forefront since 1988. Oakland Zoo is taking action to promote responsible pet ownership and to rescue and provide or find new homes for improperly owned animals. To support Oakland Zoo’s efforts to rescue and rehabilitate animals in need, please donate at oaklandzoo.org/ supportanimals. pages.text: Wednesday, February 28, 2024 27 Features your Garden column by Josh Harkinson I have made some mistakes as a gardener. The biggest was planting a vegetable garden next to a 30-foot-tall oak tree. My wife insisted on it, but in all fairness, I’m the one who ran an irrigation line next to the trunk and didn’t notice for months that it was leaking. The oak was already weak. Though we’d cut down the invasive acacia trees that had blocked its sun, the irrigation caused it to develop root rot disease, an arborist later confirmed. (You should never water oaks in the summer). The leaves began dropping. I had to blow off the driveway almost daily. I held out hope for a turnaround—until a winter storm knocked it onto the roof of my neighbor’s Volkswagen Jetta. Not watering oak trees is easier said than done, especially if you have eight of them like I do. Almost anything I plant will be next to one. Eventually I found a solution: California natives. I’ve come to love my native plants. They’re usually low maintenance, easy on my water bill, and attract birds and bees. Early spring is a great time to plant them. In the sunny parts of my yard I grow ceonothus, the California lilac. There are some 50 species of this hardy shrub, ranging from the low-growing Ceonothus thyrsiflorus (creeping blue blossom) to the tree-like Ceonothus dark star, which in my yard grew more than 7 feet tall. All of them produce dense, brilliantly blue flowers in the spring, creating a bonanza for pollinators. Their only downside is that they don’t live very long – 10 years supposedly, but in my experience closer to five. Be sure to plant them in well-drained soil. For showy blooms later in the summer, try the freakishly gigantic matilija poppy. Also known as the California tree poppy, it grows an astounding 6 to 8 feet tall and wide. You won’t need to water it after it’s established, but you will need to keep its rhizomes from invading other parts of your garden and cut the whole plant down to the ground in the winter to promote spring flowering. I know that’s a lot of work, but the prolific yellow and white flowers are worth it. Four to 9 inches in diameter, they resemble sunny-side-up eggs. No wonder it was once in the running to be the state flower. For shadier areas under oak trees, I love ribes sanguinium, or the red-flowering currant. This deciduous shrub grows six feet tall (sometimes more) and in the spring produces delightful pink flowers on dangling racemes. In the summer the flowers turn into currants that are too bitter for humans but a hit with birds. The western redbud also puts on a nice show this time of year. For a low-growing, shade-tolerant plant, I’ve found success with the evergreen ribes viburnifolium, or Catalina currant, which quickly extends branches along the ground horizontally. Also worth mentioning for dry shade: the thimbleberry, with its big attractive leaves and red fruit – like a drier version of a raspberry – that were once a staple for Native Americans. Many California natives can eventually take on an unkempt, scraggly look if you don’t prune them. Personally, I like a bit of the wild feel, especially when it comes with foraging squirrels and blue jays, fluttering butterflies, and nesting Cooper’s hawks. Still, I feel no need to apologize to those squirrels for killing that oak tree given all the tomatoes, strawberries, and sunflowers they’ve stolen from our vegetable garden since then. I think we can call it even. articles.text: Nicholas “Nick” Baz, artist, father of six, died at his home in Eugene, Oregon on February 8, 2024. He was 78. Originally from Los Gatos, and a long time resident of Eugene, Oregon and Piedmont, California, Nick specialized in painting and printmaking, and had a unique, often intense symbolic expressionistic style. Many of his works are rife with deep spiritual themes, documenting his journey through life with religious imagery. Those who knew him may recall the bright, psychedelic colors of his paintings or the distinctive smell of his turpentine-based oil medium, which perfumed his studio. Born in Toledo, Ohio on October 6, 1945, he was the son of Toufic and Virginia Baz (née Little). Toufic immigrated from Lebanon after Nick’s grandfather died in the 1918 flu pandemic. Nick was the middle of three children, with an older brother, Chris, and a younger sister, Shawn. When he was young, he moved to California. Nick attended Los Gatos High School, where he met Sara Stanley, though the two did not form a relationship until after he graduated in 1964. They married in Santa Barbara in 1968, and their first child of six children was born the next year, Charis, Bronwyn, Rose, Alyssa, Zachary, and Naomi. In 1973, the couple moved to Eugene, Oregon and four years later Nick began what would become a 30-year career in broadcasting, working as a control room engineer for KEZI. During this time, Nick pursued further education for his lifelong artistic pursuits, graduating from the University of Oregon in 1992 with a baccalaureate degree in fine art. For most of his time in Eugene, Nick painted and lived in the Friendly St. neighborhood and attended Saint Mary’s Episcopal Church. After 40 years of marriage, Nick and Sara divorced in 2009, and he never remarried. The two maintained a friendly relationship and close ties to the family they built together. In 2008, Nick moved to the Bay Area, where he worked and lived on the premises of Piedmont Community Church as its Doorkeeper. He became an active member of the Men’s Bible Study which met every Saturday morning to discuss the inspiring Biblical writings of the Old and New Testament. During these group discussions, whenever Nick spoke, you could hear a pin drop because everyone appreciated the sincere and profound faith of this beloved member of their community. When word arrived of Nick’s death, Piedmont Community Church’s Associate Pastor, Don Ashburn, wrote, “Nick was one of the most deeply spiritual people I’ve ever known. I mean that both in the sense of his devotion to God as well as his concern for the spirits and wellbeing of other people.” The members of the Men’s Bible Study shared Pastor Ashburn’s feelings. After Nick was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in 2020, he began a courageous battle against it. When his doctors recommended regular walks following chemotherapy, Nick asked the members of the Men’s Bible Study if any of them wanted to walk with him and many eagerly accepted that invitation. Among the seventeen e-mail comments the church received about Nick’s passing, many mentioned the importance of Nick’s insights during these walks. Some examples were, “I cherished those days Nick Baz, the doorkeeper at Piedmont Community Church starting in 2008, died on February 8 in Eugene, Oregon. we took our walks (as healing for me as him)”, and “Nick has been so open and honest and generous with all of us it feels we are the ones who benefited while giving him support.” He made many friends in Piedmont, and towards the end of his residency there, Nick held an art show where he sold some of his paintings before moving back to Eugene in 2021. In 2022, he took a trip to France, where he painted plein air watercolor landscapes. When he returned to the U.S., those paintings spearheaded a sold-out art show in Oakland. After an unusually long battle with cancer, Nick died in his home on the morning of February 8, 2024, surrounded by people he loved. Nick Baz is survived by all six children along with 12 grandchildren. Nick’s art may be viewed on his website: nicholasbazart.com. A Celebration of Nick’s Life will be held on Saturday, March 16, 2024 from 2:00 to 4:00 pm in the Guild Hall at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, CA.

articles.text: March 8 is International Women’s Day, a day for celebrating all the accomplishments of women around the globe. But many women still need to make up ground in one key area: retirement security. Women’s challenges in achieving a secure retirement are due to several factors, including these: • Pay gap – It’s smaller than it once was, but a wage gap still exists between men and women. In fact, women earn, on average, about 82 cents for every dollar that men earn, according to the Census Bureau. And even though this gap narrows considerably at higher educational levels, it’s still a source of concern. Women who earn less than men will likely contribute less to 401(k) plans and will ultimately see smaller Social Security checks. • Longer lives – At age 65, women live, on average, about 20 more years, compared to almost 17 for men, according to the Social Security Administration. Those extra years mean extra expenses. • Caregiving responsibilities – Traditionally, women have done much of the caregiving for young children and older parents. And while this caregiving is done with love, it also comes with financial sacrifice. Consider this: The average employment-related costs for mothers providing unpaid care is nearly $300,000 over a lifetime, according to the U.S. Department of Labor — which translates to a reduction of 15% of lifetime earnings. Furthermore, time away from the workforce results in fewer contributions to 401(k) and other employer-sponsored retirement plans. Ultimately, these issues can leave women with a retirement security deficit. Here are some moves that can help close this gap: • Contribute as much as possible to retirement plans. Try to contribute as much as you can afford to your 401(k) or similar employer-sponsored retirement plan. Your earnings can grow tax deferred and your contributions can lower your taxable income. (With a Roth 401(k), contributions aren’t deductible, but earnings and withdrawals are tax free, provided you meet certain conditions.) At a minimum, contribute enough to earn your employer’s matching contribution, if one is offered, and try to boost your contributions whenever your salary goes up. If you don’t have access to a 401(k), but you have earned income, you can contribute to an IRA. Even if you don’t have earned income, but you have a spouse who does, you might be eligible to contribute to a spousal IRA. • Maximize Social Security benefits. You can start taking Social Security at 62, but your monthly checks will be much bigger if you can afford to wait until your full retirement age, which will be around 66½. If you are married, you may want to coordinate your benefits with those of your spouse — in some cases, it makes sense for the spouse with the lower benefits to claim first, based on their earnings record, and apply for spousal benefits later, when the spouse with higher benefits begins to collect. • Build an emergency fund. Try to build an emergency fund containing up to six months’ worth of living expenses, with the money kept in a liquid account. Having this fund available will help protect you from having to dip into your retirement accounts for large, unexpected costs, such as a major home or car repair. It’s unfortunate, but women still must travel a more difficult road than men to reach retirement security. But making the right moves can help ease the journey. articles.title: How can women bridge the retirement gap?

articles.text: Rosanne Shaffer, better known and loved by all as Randi, passed away peacefully at her Piedmont home on the evening of February 18. It was her 89th birthday. Born on February 18, 1935, she was the daughter of James M. Flaherty and Nell Curran and grew up in Tulsa, Oklahoma with her two sisters, Mary Ellen and Sheila. Humor was the currency of love in the Flaherty household, a trait Randi embraced wholeheartedly and shared generously throughout her life. After relocating to New York in 1946, Randi graduated from White Plains High School and received a business degree from Westbrook College in Portland, Maine. She then began a career with American Airlines as a flight attendant that spurred a lifelong love of travel and forged enduring friendships with her fellow Kiwis. In 1959, Randi met and married the love of her life, Ron Shaffer. For 49 years, until Ron’s passing in 2012, they made Piedmont their home. With the arrival of their three children, Curran, Brad and Grant, family formed the bedrock of their life together. The Shaffer house thrived on a vibrant blend of humor and heart. Between Ron’s dry wit and Randi’s clever quips, laughter and joy filled every Randi often mused about her own obituary, saying, “Make sure you say I was funny.” She was funny. And kind and generous and mischievous and sporty. And really funny. In the great cocktail party of the afterlife, Randi is undoubtedly making fast friends, armed with a warm smile, a snappy one-liner and a Scotch on the rocks. Randi is survived by her children Curran Burfeind (David Burfeind) of Falmouth, Maine, Brad Shaffer (Tiffanie Shaffer) of Tiburon and Grant Shaffer (Alan Cumming) of New York City, She is also survived by five grandchildren that she adored: Connor, Grant, Riley, Zackary and Naimah; along with a brother-in-law and many nieces and nephews. She will be missed dearly by her family and an incredible group of friends whose compassion and devotion meant the world to her. She leaves a void that will be filled with echoes of her laughter and a readiness to find humor and joy in every moment. At Randi’s request, no memorial is planned at this time. In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to The Cancer League in Oakland, Sutter VNA & Hospice in Emeryville or the charity of your choice. Randi operated on a firstname basis with the world, and her sense of humor was a gift she shared freely. She was a cherished member of various community groups in Piedmont, from the Garden Club to Hollyhock to The Cancer League – always ready to lend a hand or a joke, often blurring the lines between the two. Randi’s faith was a constant source of strength, and the Corpus Christi Church community remained a mainstay in her life.

He was 78. Originally from Los Gatos, and a long time resident of Eugene, Oregon and Piedmont, California, Nick specialized in painting and printmaking, and had a unique, often intense symbolic expressionistic style. Many of his works are rife with deep spiritual themes, documenting his journey through life with religious imagery. Those who knew him may recall the bright, psychedelic colors of his paintings or the distinctive smell of his turpentine-based oil medium, which perfumed his studio. Born in Toledo, Ohio on October 6, 1945, he was the son of Toufic and Virginia Baz (née Little). Toufic immigrated from Lebanon after Nick’s grandfather died in the 1918 flu pandemic. Nick was the middle of three children, with an older brother, Chris, and a younger sister, Shawn. When he was young, he moved to California. Nick attended Los Gatos High School, where he met Sara Stanley, though the two did not form a relationship until after he graduated in 1964. They married in Santa Barbara in 1968, and their first child of six children was born the next year, Charis, Bronwyn, Rose, Alyssa, Zachary, and Naomi. In 1973, the couple moved to Eugene, Oregon and four years later Nick began what would become a 30-year career in broadcasting, working as a control room engineer for KEZI. During this time, Nick pursued further education for his lifelong artistic pursuits, graduating from the University of Oregon in 1992 with a baccalaureate degree in fine art. For most of his time in Eugene, Nick painted and lived in the Friendly St. neighborhood and attended Saint Mary’s Episcopal Church. After 40 years of marriage, Nick and Sara divorced in 2009, and he never remarried. The two maintained a friendly relationship and close ties to the family they built together. In 2008, Nick moved to the Bay Area, where he worked and lived on the premises of Piedmont Community Church as its Doorkeeper. He became an active member of the Men’s Bible Study which met every Saturday morning to discuss the inspiring Biblical writings of the Old and New Testament. During these group discussions, whenever Nick spoke, you could hear a pin drop because everyone appreciated the sincere and profound faith of this beloved member of their community. When word arrived of Nick’s death, Piedmont Community Church’s Associate Pastor, Don Ashburn, wrote, “Nick was one of the most deeply spiritual people I’ve ever known. I mean that both in the sense of his devotion to God as well as his concern for the spirits and wellbeing of other people.” The members of the Men’s Bible Study shared Pastor Ashburn’s feelings. After Nick was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in 2020, he began a courageous battle against it. When his doctors recommended regular walks following chemotherapy, Nick asked the members of the Men’s Bible Study if any of them wanted to walk with him and many eagerly accepted that invitation. Among the seventeen e-mail comments the church received about Nick’s passing, many mentioned the importance of Nick’s insights during these walks. Some examples were, “I cherished those days Nick Baz, the doorkeeper at Piedmont Community Church starting in 2008, died on February 8 in Eugene, Oregon. we took our walks (as healing for me as him)”, and “Nick has been so open and honest and generous with all of us it feels we are the ones who benefited while giving him support.” He made many friends in Piedmont, and towards the end of his residency there, Nick held an art show where he sold some of his paintings before moving back to Eugene in 2021. In 2022, he took a trip to France, where he painted plein air watercolor landscapes. When he returned to the U.S., those paintings spearheaded a sold-out art show in Oakland. After an unusually long battle with cancer, Nick died in his home on the morning of February 8, 2024, surrounded by people he loved. Nick Baz is survived by all six children along with 12 grandchildren. Nick’s art may be viewed on his website: nicholasbazart.com. A Celebration of Nick’s Life will be held on Saturday, March 16, 2024 from 2:00 to 4:00 pm in the Guild Hall at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, CA. Longtime Piedmonter Randi Shaffer dies at 89 Rosanne Shaffer, better known and loved by all as Randi, passed away peacefully at her Piedmont home on the evening of February 18. It was her 89th birthday. Born on February 18, 1935, she was the daughter of James M. Flaherty and Nell Curran and grew up in Tulsa, Oklahoma with her two sisters, Mary Ellen and Sheila. Humor was the currency of love in the Flaherty household, a trait Randi embraced wholeheartedly and shared generously throughout her life. After relocating to New York in 1946, Randi graduated from White Plains High School and received a business degree from Westbrook College in Portland, Maine. She then began a career with American Airlines as a flight attendant that spurred a lifelong love of travel and forged enduring friendships with her fellow Kiwis. In 1959, Randi met and married the love of her life, Ron Shaffer. For 49 years, until Ron’s passing in 2012, they made Piedmont their home. With the arrival of their three children, Curran, Brad and Grant, family formed the bedrock of their life together. The Shaffer house thrived on a vibrant blend of humor and heart. Between Ron’s dry wit and Randi’s clever quips, laughter and joy filled every Randi often mused about her own obituary, saying, “Make sure you say I was funny.” She was funny. And kind and generous and mischievous and sporty. And really funny. In the great cocktail party of the afterlife, Randi is undoubtedly making fast friends, armed with a warm smile, a snappy one-liner and a Scotch on the rocks. Randi is survived by her children Curran Burfeind (David Burfeind) of Falmouth, Maine, Brad Shaffer (Tiffanie Shaffer) of Tiburon and Grant Shaffer (Alan Cumming) of New York City, She is also survived by five grandchildren that she adored: Connor, Grant, Riley, Zackary and Naimah; along with a brother-in-law and many nieces and nephews. She will be missed dearly by her family and an incredible group of friends whose compassion and devotion meant the world to her. She leaves a void that will be filled with echoes of her laughter and a readiness to find humor and joy in every moment. At Randi’s request, no memorial is planned at this time. In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to The Cancer League in Oakland, Sutter VNA & Hospice in Emeryville or the charity of your choice. March 8 is International Women’s Day, a day for celebrating all the accomplishments of women around the globe. But many women still need to make up ground in one key area: retirement security. Women’s challenges in achieving a secure retirement are due to several factors, including these: • Pay gap – It’s smaller than it once was, but a wage gap still exists between men and women. In fact, women earn, on average, about 82 cents for every dollar that men earn, according to the Census Bureau. And even though this gap narrows considerably at higher educational levels, it’s still a source of concern. Women who earn less than men will likely contribute less to 401(k) plans and will ultimately see smaller Social Security checks. • Longer lives – At age 65, women live, on average, about 20 more years, compared to almost 17 for men, according to the Social Security Administration. Those extra years mean extra expenses. • Caregiving responsibilities – Traditionally, women have done much of the caregiving for young children and older parents. And while this caregiving is done with love, it also comes with financial sacrifice. Consider this: The average employment-related costs for mothers providing unpaid care is nearly $300,000 over a lifetime, according to the U.S. Department of Labor — which translates to a reduction of 15% of lifetime earnings. Furthermore, time away from the workforce results in fewer contributions to 401(k) and other employer-sponsored retirement plans. Ultimately, these issues can leave women with a retirement security deficit. Here are some moves that can help close this gap: • Contribute as much as possible to retirement plans. Try to contribute as much as you can afford to your 401(k) or similar employer-sponsored retirement plan. Your earnings can grow tax deferred and your contributions can lower your taxable income. (With a Roth 401(k), contributions aren’t deductible, but earnings and withdrawals are tax free, provided you meet certain conditions.) At a minimum, contribute enough to earn your employer’s matching contribution, if one is offered, and try to boost your contributions whenever your salary goes up. If you don’t have access to a 401(k), but you have earned income, you can contribute to an IRA. Even if you don’t have earned income, but you have a spouse who does, you might be eligible to contribute to a spousal IRA. • Maximize Social Security benefits. You can start taking Social Security at 62, but your monthly checks will be much bigger if you can afford to wait until your full retirement age, which will be around 66½. If you are married, you may want to coordinate your benefits with those of your spouse — in some cases, it makes sense for the spouse with the lower benefits to claim first, based on their earnings record, and apply for spousal benefits later, when the spouse with higher benefits begins to collect. • Build an emergency fund. Try to build an emergency fund containing up to six months’ worth of living expenses, with the money kept in a liquid account. Having this fund available will help protect you from having to dip into your retirement accounts for large, unexpected costs, such as a major home or car repair. It’s unfortunate, but women still must travel a more difficult road than men to reach retirement security. But making the right moves can help ease the journey. articles.text: It’s time to save the date for the third annual Piedmont Food Fest. The Bay Area’s most vibrant multicultural festival is returning to Piedmont Park on Saturday, April 20 from 11 am to 4 pm. This volunteer event created post-pandemic three years ago as a way to build community through diverse food, drink, and music has evolved into a broader showcase of the Bay’s most distinctive cuisines, cultural performances, and community groups that has attracted over 3000 attendees and generated over $100,000 for local businesses. Attendees have appreciated the chance to spend the day connecting with each other amid a medley of flavors, sounds, and cultures – all gathered in one place. “Piedmont Food Fest was an absolute treat for the whole family! A not to miss community event centered around connection and diversity.” remarked Havens School parent Katie Castles Shaffer. “We love the Piedmont Food Fest! Being able to spend an afternoon with friends and community and have our kids entertained with the Kids Zone makes this an event we’ll look forward to every year. We especially appreciate the organizers’ dedication to having diverse representation across food, vendors and entertainment.” said Piedmont resident Amanda Feldman. Piedmont Food Fest 3 will feature over 17 food vendors including Crazy Empanadas, Robert Dorsey Catering, La Santa Torta, Momolicious, Arthur Mac’s, Lahor Di Khushboo, The Chairman, and Oakland Bloom as well as beer & wine tasting from local favorites including Federation Brewing, Two Broads Ciderworks, and Deer Hill Vineyards. Main stage performances will include Purple Silk Youth Orchestra, Oakland Taiko, O Hina’aro Tahitian Dance & Music, Beloved Little Circus, and the Hiiiwav Black Artist Incubator. Junior food festers can look forward to an enhanced KidZone with both carnival and multicultural craft stations. To sign up, visit www.piedmontfoodfest.org, Check out Early Bird specials available through March. This event is free to attend and all are encouraged to invite friends and family for this memorable day in Piedmont. Roger Tsai is the principal organizer of Piedmont Food Fest. Until 1940 U.S. audiences got a taste of the banquet with the touring Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo doing Act Two only, paired with “Scheherazade,” in sleek one-nighters. Piedmont Real Estate Update February 2024 Did You Know? Over the past year, our monthly newsletter has focused on data, statistics, and market trends relative to Piedmont real estate, designed to give homeowners and potential buyers a deeper look at the marketplace. This month, we thought it would be interesting to share high-level information regarding two topics that may affect you as a current or future Piedmont property owner. People may not know that the city has, among other things, information and guidelines around rental properties and requirements for running a business out of your home available on their website. If you have recently purchased a home in Piedmont, it would be helpful to connect with the city to learn more about how it runs and what you can do to make your time here more pleasurable. If you want to know more, the City Code is available at Piedmont.city.gov, and the City Clerk’s Office is a helpful resource. Short-Term Rental Requirements (such as VRBO or Airbnb): A short-term rental is defined as less than 30 consecutive days with at least two consecutive nights and not more than 60 days in a calendar year. Other factors to consider: The rented space must be a part of the primary residence and cannot be in an ADU (whether permitted or unintended). They also cannot be located in a multi-family property. The short-term rental may be hosted or unhosted. A permit is required. When applying for the permit, you’ll need owner consent, evidence of insurance, and proof that the short-term dwelling meets safety requirements (smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, etc.). To renew a permit, you must apply before the expiration of your current permit. Business tax is required on any income earned. *Source: City of Piedmont website and City Code Rentals and Investment Properties Whether you’re buying a property in Piedmont as an investment or considering a short-term rental for your own use, there are some important facts to consider. Long-Term Rental Requirements:* Long-term rentals (30 days or more) are often a good option for people looking to provide housing or live in Piedmont themselves for the community, services, or schools. Below are a few things to remember as you consider a rental property: If you’re looking to rent a property that you own, the city requires homeowners to file an Intent to Rent form and pay annual rental tax. An annual business license is required each year on property that is rented or leased. The city of Piedmont does not have a rent control ordinance. However, Piedmont is in Alameda County, which may have rent and eviction controls that housing providers should consider. As always, if you are considering renting a property, we suggest you research the local laws and speak with an attorney if needed. Did you know the Piedmont Unified School District and the City of Piedmont are separate entities? Before signing a lease, contact the school district to learn more about the enrollment process and get tips for a successful transition into the school system. Home-Based Businesses In Piedmont, home occupation means a business conducted at a residence (a definition that doesn’t include renting a property), and comes with some regulation. The goal of the regulation is to accommodate the liberty to conduct economic activity in a home while preserving the residential feel of the neighborhood. The requirements are listed below, but we highly recommend contacting the City Clerk’s office for more detailed information and guidelines. Application to the City Clerk together with a fee; Notify adjacent residents of the intention to conduct a home business. Review of the application. No more than one room in the residence may be used in connection with the home occupation. Issuance of a home occupation permit. Business license tax.
